rv.q: This is a storm of a show which can easily be re-envisaged for the West End.
I was hoping for a similarly intoxicating blast from Sylvia... with so much political kerosene to burn, Kate Prince's show is too often dampened by its own virtue.
The result is fast and fearsome, pounding with kinetic energy.
Hawley’s marvellous songs are more planted than propelling.
Breathless hip-hop history of the suffragette movement is broad, but at times exhilarating
Still, just as that vote was hard-won, Sylvia still feels a few slogging steps short of victory.

For all its flaws, it’s never anything less than exciting to watch, thanks to the wit and dynamism of Prince’s choreography, the formidable talents of this note-perfect cast, and powerful songs enlivened with nice little references to everyone from Aretha Franklin to Eminem.
There will doubtless be an audience for this poppy, peppy, pappy piece of work, but the Pankhursts surely deserve better.
It’s still messy, but the good news is that the soul singer Beverley Knight returns in the role of Emmeline.
It's a brave and vibrant hit at the Old Vic.
It was perhaps predictable after Hamilton took the world by storm, that a steady stream of hip-hop fusion stage musicals would follow in its wake.
Yet ultimately it feels overstuffed – too much telling, not enough dramatising.

cn.t: This hip-hop suffragette musical earns praise for its energy, choreography, and Beverley Knight's performance, but critics find it overstuffed and too polite, falling short of Hamilton comparisons despite admirable ambitions.

vr.q: On the strength of the overall presentation of the performances that it is a four-star piece of theater.
